issues.legal_issue: A payment received under a lease covenant that exceeds the public cess legally payable by the recipient is taxable income when it is received and appropriated as a contractual payment.
material_facts: The lease required the lessee to pay public taxes and assessments, including amounts the lessor had to pay.
The lessee paid amounts calculated as a share of rent and royalty, believing that this was required by the lease.
The amounts received substantially exceeded the public cess legally payable on the leased lands.
The recipient received and appropriated the payments under the lease, rather than collecting them as an agent for the government.
The recipient’s liability to pay the legally due cess was not a liability of the lessee as an inferior holder.
issues.conclusion: The amounts exceeding the cess legally payable were income and were taxable; the amount of cess the recipient was legally liable to pay was not subject to income tax.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of income in section 2(6C) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is inclusive. Anything properly described as income is taxable unless expressly exempted (Gopal Saran Narain Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax). Payments under a covenant directly related to taxable rent and royalty may themselves be income. A payment received and appropriated as a contractual payment does not lose its character as income merely because it was made under a mistake or may later be claimed back. The legally payable cess is distinct from the excess contractual receipt.

rule.if: tax_assessment_proceeding and lease_payment_covenant and payment_received_and_appropriated and payment_exceeds_legal_cess

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: A tax authority is determining whether a receipt is taxable in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.lease_payment_covenant: A lessee agreed under a lease to pay public charges for which the lessor was liable.
predicates.payment_received_and_appropriated: The lessor received and appropriated a payment made by the lessee under the lease.
predicates.payment_exceeds_legal_cess: The payment made by the lessee exceeded the public cess legally payable by the lessor.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment concerns a payment received and appropriated under a lease covenant and that payment exceeds the lessor’s legally payable cess, the excess is taxable income.

issues.legal_issue: A tax authority may determine the amount of public cess legally payable by a taxpayer when that determination is relevant to an income-tax assessment, even if the public body is not a party to the assessment.
material_facts: The amount of legally payable cess was relevant to deciding which part of the lessee’s payment was income.
The tax authority had to determine the recipient’s legal liability to pay cess on the lands.
The government or local board was not made a party to the tax assessment proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The tax authority could determine the amount of cess legally payable in the assessment proceeding; the absence of the government or local board as a party did not prevent that determination.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing income tax, the income-tax authority has jurisdiction to decide whether a receipt is income and to determine matters properly arising for that assessment. The authority need not join another person or body concerned with the receipt, even though its determination may not bind that person or body in a separate matter.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: A tax authority is conducting an income-tax assessment of a taxpayer.
predicates.cess_amount_relevant: The amount of public cess legally payable by the taxpayer affects the assessment of a receipt.
predicates.public_body_not_party: The public body concerned with the cess is not a party to the tax assessment.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment depends on the amount of cess legally payable, the assessing authority may determine that amount even if the public body is not a party.

issues.legal_issue: A receipt is not exempt as casual and non-recurring income when it is not shown to be accidental or fortuitous and its non-recurring character is not established.
material_facts: The recipient claimed exemption under section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the payments were casual and non-recurring.
The payments arose from the lessee’s contractual payments under the lease.
The receipt was not produced by chance, accident, or an unforeseen source of income.
The recipient did not establish that the receipt was non-recurring; the contention had been abandoned before the Tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) as income of a casual and non-recurring nature.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, exempts income of a casual and non-recurring nature. A contractual receipt that is not accidental, fortuitous, or from an unforeseen source, and is not shown to be non-recurring, does not qualify for that exemption.

rule.if: income_tax_exemption_proceeding and contractual_receipt and not chance_or_accidental_receipt and not_shown_nonrecurring

predicates.income_tax_exemption_proceeding: A taxpayer seeks exemption from income tax on the ground that a receipt is casual and non-recurring.
predicates.contractual_receipt: The recipient obtained the payment under a contractual obligation.
predicates.chance_or_accidental_receipt: The receipt arose by chance or accident, rather than through an established source.
predicates.not_shown_nonrecurring: The recipient did not establish that the receipt was non-recurring.

issues.definition: A contractual receipt is not exempt as casual and non-recurring when it did not arise by chance or accident and its non-recurring nature was not established.
